- world.insert_components {entity, components:{name:value}}: insert or replace components. Also world.mutate_components has the same parameters. Writes Transform, Visibility and light components. Animation tracks or a parent overwrite a part's Transform each frame, so move static parts.
- world.query {components:[names], has:[names], name, limit}: query entities, returning selected components and optionally filtering by required components or name.
- world.spawn_entity {components, shape, position}: create a visible runtime entity. shape may be {kind:"box", size:[x,y,z]}, {kind:"sphere", radius}, or {kind:"cylinder", radius, height}; shape also accepts color:[r,g,b], emissive, metallic, roughness and opacity.
- world.despawn_entity {entity}: remove an entity spawned by this tool or an authored part.
- world.bounds {entity}: return its world-space {center, size}; Transform is only an offset from where the part was built.
- animation.set_float {part, name, value}, animation.set_bool {part, name, value}, animation.trigger {part, name}: drive an animation state machine.
- water.disturb {part?, x, z, radius?, amount?, splash?}: disturb sim-enabled water under the point; default radius 0.5 m, amount 0.04 m. A positive amount above 0.03 m also emits a splash unless splash is false (default true). Omitted part targets every sim water part under the point.
- water.status {}: return {parts: [{name, resolution, cell, steps, time, max_abs, volume, wet_cells}]} for simulated water. Resolution is the longest grid side, cell is spacing in metres, steps counts fixed steps since construction, time is simulated seconds, max_abs is peak absolute displacement in metres, volume is signed displaced cubic metres, wet_cells counts water cells. Empty parts when no water simulates.
- water.height {x, z}: return {height}, simulated displacement plus procedural wave height in metres.
- sim.status {}: every running simulation program (sim.program nodes, one per part and per copy of a character): {sims: [{part, mode, rate, elements, steps, params, states, bones, min, max, fingerprint, error}]}. mode is "particles" (tetrahedra) or "mesh" (drives the vertices of its input mesh); min and max are the box the points fill; fingerprint is a hash of the whole state (equal fingerprints mean equal simulations, so use it to check that a change did or did not alter the result); error is null or the message that stopped the program (a kernel wrote another element, an index outside an array, too much work).
- sim.step {part?, steps}: advance the programs of the part (all when omitted) by that many fixed steps now (1/rate seconds each, at most 10,000), feeding them the current bone poses, and answer like sim.status. Use it to run a simulation to a state and then measure it, without waiting for frames.
- sim.set_param {part?, name, values}: set a param of a running program (values: a number or an array of numbers); it keeps the value until sim.reset. sim.reset {part?}: start the program again from its initial state.
- fx.burst {name, position, scale}: emit one-shot particles (explode, sparks, smoke, dust, fire, splash, magic, steam, embers).
- physics.raycast {origin:[x,y,z], direction:[x,y,z], max_distance=100, mask?}: play mode only. The first physics body a ray meets: {hit:false} or {hit:true, part, node, point, normal, distance}. For aiming, line of sight, hitscan shots and "is the floor under me". Only parts with phys.body (and limp ragdoll bones) can be hit.
- physics.overlap {center:[x,y,z], radius}: play mode only. {parts:[{part, node}]} that have a physics body inside the sphere (an explosion's victims, a proximity check).
- To make a ragdoll start from play (a button, a thrown ball, a timer), put behavior.on(trigger="select"|"collide"|"timer"|..., action="ragdoll", target="<the phys.ragdoll name>") on any part: no clip is needed.
- physics.ragdoll {name, impulse?:[x,y,z]}: play mode only. Makes the character whose phys.ragdoll is called name go limp from its current pose, with an optional shove on its root bone (a shot, a blast: try [0,0,-40] for a hard push); it falls and tumbles on every phys.body and stands again when play stops. {bones:n}.
- ground.sample {x, z}: sample ground at a point.
- ground.profile {from:[x,z], to:[x,z], samples}: sample a line across declared game terrain, reporting height, normal, surface, decel and bounce; height is null over a void.
- world.batch {ops:[{method, params}]}: run up to 512 world calls in one request.

Component reflection is cheap for edits and inspection, but use scripts for animating thousands of things every frame. The world must be on screen and running.
topics.materials:
Flat colour reads as a toy. These surface programs are tested (each bakes in the viewer) and use a texture expression language you can also edit. Use one by pasting its
program into solid.texture@1 after a solid.material, with the tile it lists (metres per repeat). tile is required for merged, scattered or procedural meshes: they carry no UVs, so the
texture is projected in world space. Example:
  trunk_m = solid.material@1(trunk, color=[0.3, 0.2, 0.14], roughness=0.95)
  trunk_t = solid.texture@1(trunk_m, program="<a program below>", tile=1.2, size="512")
A program that fails to bake is reported by check as texture.bake_failed with the node and the reason (texture_nodes lists the node catalog). Mirrored coordinates keep tiles seamless,
so a close look shows mirror symmetry; vary the tile between neighbouring parts to hide it. Each distinct program costs one texture layer; the viewer has about 32.

topics.characters:
make_character builds a whole animated character. It writes the graph for you (a smooth body from tapered bones, a rig, skinning,
walk / run / idle clips, toon shading), so you do not build limbs one node at a time.

  make_character(plan="biped", sliders={size: 1.7, head: 1.2, legs: 1.1, color: [0.95, 0.8, 0.7]})
  make_character(plan="quadruped", sliders={size: 2.4, horns: true, wings: true}, name="dragon")
  make_character(plan="serpent", sliders={size: 3, tail: 1.3})

plan: biped, quadruped or serpent. sliders: size in metres (a serpent's is its length), head, limbs, torso, legs, neck, tail as
multipliers 0.5 to 2, color [r, g, b], horns and wings for a quadruped. name keeps several characters apart (up to 13 lowercase
letters and digits); at = [x, y, z] places one. Call it again with another name for more characters.

For a body no plan covers, give creature = { name, color, bones: [...], blobs: [...] }. A bone is { name, parent, head, tail, radius:
[at head, at tail], role, pair, phase }. The creature stands on y = 0 and faces +z. role (leg, arm, spine, neck, head, tail, wing, free)
picks how it moves. pair=true means you wrote the +x side and the left and right copies are made (name_l, name_r). A bone's parent must
come earlier in the list; at most 32 rig bones (a pair counts twice), chains at most 8 deep. blobs are rounded lumps with no bone
(a head, a chest): { name, center, radii }. Errors name the bone or slider to change.

Afterwards: frame_view, and solid.style on the part named after the character to change its look (see topic styles).
topics.styles:
Looks. solid.style@1(solid, style="anime"|"realistic"|"painterly"|"flat"|"retro"|"ink", outline_scale=1) sets shading, outline and
texture finishing in one word and keeps colour, roughness and textures. realistic removes an earlier style. solid.toon@1 gives
exact control of the cel bands (bands, feather, shadow colour, rim, spec, outline). Put either after solid.material / solid.texture.

Non-repeating textures: solid.texture@1(..., tile=2, no_repeat=true, no_repeat_scale=1) blends three shifted samples to hide visible repeats on large surfaces. no_repeat defaults to false; no_repeat_scale is grid cells per tile (0.25..8, default 1), with larger values making smaller patches. Low quality uses a single sample.

Textures that follow the shape. A solid.texture program can use surface nodes, which read the part's own geometry:
  surface_convex(gain)   1 on sharp outer edges: edge wear, chipped paint
  surface_cavity(gain)   1 in creases and dents: dirt, grime
  surface_up(power)      1 on tops, 0 on walls: moss, snow, dust
  surface_ao(strength)   ambient occlusion; surface_curvature(gain) signed; surface_height(low, high) height above the ground
Example (stone with pale worn edges, dark creases and moss on top):
  solid.texture@1(block, program="ao = surface_ao(strength=0.35); stone = colorize(ao, gradient=[0:#4a4038, 1:#a8978a]); moss = colorize(ao, gradient=[0:#2e4a1c, 1:#78a83e]); wear = colorize(ao, gradient=[0:#a79b8a, 1:#efe6d4]); up = surface_up(power=3); edge = surface_convex(gain=7); a1 = blend(moss, stone, up, blend_type=normal, amount=0.9); albedo = blend(wear, a1, edge, blend_type=normal, amount=0.85)")
IMPORTANT: blend(top, bottom, mask) draws the FIRST colour where the mask is 1. blend(moss, stone, up) is moss on the tops.
Use 3D noise nodes (tex3d_fbm ...) with surface nodes: a 2D noise shows seams between the part's UV charts.
topics.fields:
A pattern is a function of position, written as a short program. field.expr@1(code="...") makes one; scatter.place@1 takes it as its
third input (where) and multiplies it into the planting density: 1 plants as usual, 0 plants nothing, between thins out.

  w = field.expr@1(code="out = step(8.0, p.y) * (1.0 - step(18.0, p.y))")      only between 8 and 18 m high
  f = scatter.place@1(tree, ground, w, radius=3, seed=2, max_slope=35)

Inside code: p (world position, vec3), n (surface normal), uv, the numbers pi and tau, vector types vec2/vec3/vec4, and the results of other
patterns linked as inputs a, b, c, d (field.expr@1(a_node, b_node, code="out = a * (1.0 - b)")). Functions: abs sign floor ceil fract sqrt exp log pow
sin cos atan2 min max clamp mix step smoothstep length distance select(condition, a, b), the % operator, and noise: perlin, fbm, ridged. The
program must assign out; statements are separated by ";" (a = p.x * 2.0; out = a + 1.0). Keep it under about 256 operations.
Patterns are sampled per planting cell, so the thinning follows the ground, not the grid.

Variation per copy: inst.vary@1(set, scale=p1, yaw=p2, lift=p3) gives every placement its own size, turn about up (radians) and height from
patterns sampled where it stands (each optional). Noise makes natural differences:
  s = field.expr@1(code="out = 0.7 + 0.6 * (0.5 + 0.5 * perlin(p * 0.37, 3.0))")
  y = field.expr@1(code="out = 6.2831853 * fract(perlin(p * 1.9, 5.0) * 7.0)")
  trees = inst.vary@1(forest, scale=s, yaw=y)

field.mask_from@1(tile, layer="flat") turns a terrain channel (made by terrain.mask) into a pattern, the same layer scatter.place's layer
parameter reads. A pattern is not geometry: link it into a node that takes one; it cannot be a scene output.
Mistakes come back as expr.error (with the position in code), pattern.not_float (a pattern must give a number) or terrain.unknown_layer.
topics.plants:
Plants are kits written in the language (list_operators ids=["kit.oak"] returns the source): oak, pine, grass_tuft. Put the kit source ahead of the
program and call it like a group: oak1 = oak(seed=3, leaf_color=[0.2, 0.42, 0.12]). They stand on y = 0 at about 10 m (oak), 9.4 m (pine), 0.45 m (grass).
Grass uses solid.foliage(grass=true): roots blend toward ground_color by ground_blend (0..1), darken near the soil and tilt their normals up.
Blades stay full size to fade_near metres and shrink to zero at fade_far; translucency (0..1) adds sunlight through their tips, and exposure_boost defaults to 1.
The grass_tuft kit enables this by default (blend 0.6, near 25, far 70, translucency 0.5); color still sets the blade colour. Set ground_color to your terrain's soil colour.
Low quality skips translucency and root occlusion. These are viewer effects; the mesh keeps its original triangles.
Plant them with scatter.place, name where each grows with patterns, and give each tree its own size with inst.vary. A mixed wood:

  t = terrain.tile@1(size=[128, 128], cell=1, seed=4, height=20, scale=90)
  g = terrain.material@1(t)
  oak1 = oak()
  pine1 = pine()
  zone = field.expr@1(code="out = step(0.0, perlin(p * 0.03, 9.0))")            1 where oaks grow
  other = field.expr@1(code="out = 1.0 - step(0.0, perlin(p * 0.03, 9.0))")     1 where pines grow
  oaks = scatter.place@1(oak1, t, zone, radius=11, seed=2, max_slope=30)
  pines = scatter.place@1(pine1, t, other, radius=8, seed=5, max_slope=30)
  size = field.expr@1(code="out = 0.7 + 0.6 * (0.5 + 0.5 * perlin(p * 0.21, 3.0))")
  oaks_v = inst.vary@1(oaks, scale=size)
  pines_v = inst.vary@1(pines, scale=size)
  output ground = g
  output oaks = oaks_v
  output pines = pines_v

Each species is its own output (an instance set has one shape). Spacing is radius in metres: 11 for broad oaks, 8 for pines, 1.5 for grass.
DETAIL: oak(edge_length=...) trades smoothness for triangles: 0.35 (default) 7,400, 0.5 4,100, 0.8 1,600, 1.2 800. pine(ragged=0.0) is a clean stack of cones, 280 triangles
instead of 2,700. Use the fine ones for the handful near the player and the lean ones for a wood: build two kits (oak1 = oak(), oak_far = oak(edge_length=1.2)), scatter
them with complementary where patterns (one near the player's start, one elsewhere), and keep inside the budget.
Terrain detail uses non-repeating sampling by default: terrain.material@1(t, no_repeat=false) turns it off for comparison. no_repeat_scale sets grid cells per detail tile (0.25..8, default 1); larger values make smaller patches. Low quality uses a single sample regardless of the flag.

BUILDINGS AND LANDMARKS BY HAND: terrain.flatten@1(t, at=[30, 40], radius=5, blend=6) levels a pad (the ground keeps its height at the centre, or
to="height", height=12 sets one) and terrain.place@1(hut, pad, at=[[30, 40], [62, 56]], yaw_scale=[[0, 1], [-35, 1]], sink=0.1) stands copies of any
shape on the ground at the x,z you list, so you never need the height. Flatten after terrain.erode (erosion rebuilds the ground and would undo the pad) and before terrain.mask, and pass the flattened tile as the
ground of terrain.place. Ropes, washing lines and chains: curve.hang@1(from=[...], to=[...], slack=0.05) then curve.tube.
REAL TREES AND SEASONS: flora.tree@1(kind="oak"|"pine"|"birch"|"willow"|"shrub"|"palm", height=9, seed=3, lod=1) grows a real tree (species bark, curved limbs, root flare,
lobed or needle leaves). season="autumn" turns the default green leaves orange and red with yellow among them, "spring" a fresh pale green, "winter" strips the leaves; a
colour you give in leaves= always wins over the season. lod 1 is half the triangles of lod 0 and is the right level for a wood.
VARIATION: an instance set has ONE shape, so a mixed planting is several scatter.place nodes that SHARE one planting: give them the same ground, radius, density and seed, the
same mix="0.45, 0.35, 0.2" and each its own pick (0, 1, 2). Every plant goes to exactly one of them (mix is the weights), so variants never overlap and their shares follow the
weights. Make the variants differ by seed, height, season or colour: oak_a = flora.tree(seed=3), oak_b = flora.tree(seed=5, leaves=[0.17, 0.4, 0.1]); oaks_a = scatter.place(oak_a,
land, radius=11, seed=2, mix="1, 1", pick=0); oaks_b = scatter.place(oak_b, land, radius=11, seed=2, mix="1, 1", pick=1). A grove in its own colours is a separate scatter with its
own where pattern (grove = field.expr(code="out = smoothstep(0.1, 0.4, perlin(p * 0.018, 21.0))") and season="autumn"). terrain.biomes@1(land) gives the layers biome_forest, biome_meadow
and biome_rock to plant by (layer="biome_forest").
GROUND KITS (put the kit source ahead, call like a group): wildflower (petal_color, centre_color, petals), fern (color, seed), mushroom (cap_color, stem_color, spot_color), log, stump,
reed (color, head_color), flowering_bush (flower_color, seed), rock (seed). Plant each in several colourings with mix and pick: a meadow is wildflower() in pink, gold, violet and white,
mix="3, 3, 2, 2", pick 0 to 3, radius 1.1. Ferns and mushrooms go under trees (layer="biome_forest"), rocks beside slopes (max_slope=50, sink=0.12, align=0.5, scale=[0.6, 2.2]), reeds
at low wet ground, logs and stumps sparsely (radius 14 to 16). The whole forest is web/tests/scenes/flora/forest.txt.
COST: an oak is about 7,400 triangles, a pine 2,700, a tuft 42, and every copy draws them all. The wood above (44 oaks, 84 pines, 4,600 tufts on
128 x 128 m) draws about 780,000 triangles, 2.6 times the provisional Quest budget of 300,000. For a headset-sized scene use radius 18 (oaks), 14
(pines) and 3 (grass): 15 oaks, 21 pines, 1,160 tufts, about 250,000 in all with the ground. Always run scene_overview or check after planting; it counts every copy.
topics.game:
A game is data. Write it as game.* nodes and join them with game.collect@1; output the joined node as "rules".

  score = game.var@1(name="score", value=0)
  hero  = game.kind@1(name="player", size=0.5, speed=4, tags=["hero"])
  coin  = game.kind@1(name="coin", size=0.4, tags=["pickup"])
  p0    = game.spawn@1(kind="player", at=[0, 0, 0])
  c0    = game.spawn@1(kind="coin", at=[3, 0, 2], count=8, spread=6)
  move  = game.input@1(name="move", axis="x,z", target="tag:hero")
  pick  = game.rule@1(on="touch", a="tag:hero", b="tag:pickup", do="add:score:1;destroy:b")
  win   = game.goal@1(outcome="win", when="score>=8")
  all   = game.collect@1(score, hero, coin, p0, c0, move, pick, win, name="coins")
  output rules = all

Write the game in this order and check each part: (1) core loop in one sentence, (2) kinds with tags (what exists), (3) spawns (where and how many; game.spawn@1(places, kind="lantern") makes one entity per placement of a set, standing exactly where each was placed, so scatter.place on
hilly ground puts pickups on the hill: spots = scatter.place@1(marker, ground, radius=26, seed=9, max_slope=15), then game.spawn@1(spots, kind="lantern"); at most 2,048),
(4) rules (on= touch, tick every=seconds, var:<name>; a= and b= select by tag:<tag> or kind:<name>; when= a condition on variables;
do= actions joined by ";": add:var:n, set:var:n, destroy:a|b, lose, win, effect:sfx:name@b), (5) goals (win/lose when a condition holds),
(6) feedback (effects): effect:sfx:coin@b plays a procedural sound where entity b stood (coin, jump, hit, explosion, laser, whoosh, click, powerup,
splash, dooropen, doorclose and more; check names any that do not exist, with the real list in its fix). Kinds draw as scene parts: game.kind(part="coin_mesh")
shows every entity of that kind with the scene output named coin_mesh (check reports a part that does not exist). Show progress with game.hud@1(text="Lanterns {score} / 4", anchor="gaze", size=0.005): a panel of plain geometry in front of the viewer whose {names} are
variables (anchors gaze, left, right, top, bottom; size is the edge of one font pixel in metres, 0.005 gives 3.5 cm letters; at most 8 panels of 64 characters).
The player is the hero:
game.input(name="walk", follow="viewer", target="tag:hero") puts the entity tagged hero where the viewer stands, so walking into a pickup touches it. Kits (a key-and-door pair, a coin kit) are game.collect nodes you can join into the final collect.

A key and a door is three rules and a variable (a rule with when= only fires when its condition holds; a door that opens is a destroyed entity):
  has_key = game.var@1(name="has_key", value=0)
  take = game.rule@1(on="touch", a="tag:hero", b="tag:key", do="add:has_key:1;destroy:b;effect:sfx:coin@b")
  open = game.rule@1(on="touch", a="tag:hero", b="tag:gate", when="has_key>=1", do="destroy:b;effect:sfx:dooropen@b")
  leave = game.rule@1(on="touch", a="tag:hero", b="tag:exit", do="win")
Kinds touch as spheres of size metres. To make a kind an obstacle give it solid=[w, h, d] (a box in metres centred on the entity): game.kind@1(name="door", size=2.0,
tags=["gate"], part="door_mesh", solid=[0.5, 2.6, 7.6]). The hero (the player) cannot walk into a live solid and is held on the side it came from, even if the viewer jumps across it;
destroying the entity (the open rule) removes the obstacle. Without solid a door is only a picture that disappears and a bot walks straight through. The player starts at the
hero's spawn, facing the first other entity.

HANDS (what makes it a VR game, not a walking game): give each hand an entity and follow a controller, and mark carryable things grab=true:
  gl = game.kind@1(name="glove_l", size=0.09, tags=["hand", "hand_l"], part="glove_mesh")
  gr = game.kind@1(name="glove_r", size=0.09, tags=["hand", "hand_r"], part="glove_mesh")
  fuse = game.kind@1(name="fuse", size=0.12, tags=["item"], part="fuse_mesh", grab=true)
  hl = game.input@1(name="left", follow="left_hand", target="tag:hand_l")      hr = same with "right_hand" and "tag:hand_r"
Squeezing a grip within reach (hand size + item size) picks up the nearest grab=true thing and carries it until the grip opens; pulling a
trigger raises a use event on what is in reach. Events: grab, release, use (a = the hand, b = the thing), plus touch as ever, and a carried
thing touches what it is brought to. A socket is a rule on touch: game.rule@1(on="touch", a="kind:fuse", b="kind:port1",
do="add:fuses:1;destroy:a;destroy:b;spawn:fuse_in@1.5,1.3,2.8;move:kind:door1:0,2.6,0;effect:sfx:dooropen@b"); a lever is a rule on use:
game.rule@1(on="use", a="tag:hand", b="kind:lever", do="destroy:b;spawn:lever_dn@x,y,z;destroy:kind:cage_gate"). Actions you can chain: add, set,
destroy, spawn:kind@x,y,z, move:selector:dx,dy,dz (a door slides up: move:kind:door1:0,2.6,0), setvel, setprop, timer:name:seconds, emit, win,
lose, effect:sfx. Centre a door's mesh on its own origin and spawn it at half its height, because its solid is centred on the entity. In
a browser without a headset the right hand floats in front of the view: hold G to grip and T to pull the trigger. A finished example with
four fuses, two doors, a lever, a cage and a reactor is web/tests/worlds/blackout.txt.

LEVELS ARE REAL LANDSCAPES, NOT BOXES. A game level outdoors is a terrain, with real plants, built from the engine's own tools; boxes for ground and spheres on sticks for trees are
a failure, not a shortcut. Ground: terrain.tile@1 (one editable tile with a height grid; use cell=0.5 or finer for anything a ball rolls on), shaped with terrain.erode, levelled
where it must be flat with terrain.flatten@1 (a pad for a tee, a green, a house; to="height" with a LOWER height digs a hollow such as a bunker or a pond bed, and the shoulder
blends back into the land), dressed with terrain.material (grass, sand, rock by slope and height), water with river.carve and river.water. Plants: flora.tree@1 species
(oak, pine, birch, willow ...) planted with scatter.place@1 over the tile (radius, seed, max_slope; use a terrain.mask zone to keep them off the playing area), grass tufts and
rocks the same way; props such as fences come from the kits (kit.fence ...; list_operators shows them). Whatever the player or a ball moves on is named in game.terrain: the
OUTPUT names of the terrain tile parts. Surfaces that change how a ball rolls (a green, a bunker) are footprint parts: a thin flat disc or pad (solid.cylinder, a few millimetres tall, a
colour of its own) set exactly on the ground with terrain.place (sink=0, at=[[x, z]]) and named in game.surface(parts=[...]); the hollow itself is the terrain.flatten. Hand-held
tools and props are modelled as the real thing: a golf club has a tapered shaft (a loft or sweep that narrows toward the head, about 14 mm to 9 mm), a rubber grip with bands, a
hosel where the shaft meets the head, and a head with a real shape (an iron: a thin blade with a sloped face and a sole; a putter: a blade or mallet with a flat face and a sight
line), bevelled edges (poly.bevel_network) and a metal or painted material; look at it close up with snapshot before you call it done. Check the whole level by flying a view
over it and by looking at it from where the player stands.

THROWING: a kind with fall=true is pulled down by gravity and rests one radius above the ground (game.ground@1(y=0.25) moves the ground, default 0); bounce=0..0.95
is how much speed it keeps off the floor. A grabbed one does not fall; let go of it while the hand swings and it leaves with the hand's velocity, so it can be thrown:
  rock = game.kind@1(name="crate", size=0.25, tags=["item"], part="crate_mesh", grab=true, fall=true, bounce=0.3)
  hit  = game.rule@1(on="touch", a="tag:item", b="tag:creature", do="stun:b:4;destroy:a;effect:particles:explode@b;effect:sfx:boom@b")
PLAYABLE HERO: game.controller@1(kind="player", speed=5, accel=40, decel=50, jump=8, gravity=24, extra_jumps=1, relative="camera", turn=720) makes a kind walk, jump (variable
height, coyote time, jump buffer, double jump) and stand on the ground and on the tops of kinds with solid=[w,h,d] (it steps up ledges lower than step=0.3). mode="walk" (3D),
"platformer" (a side-scroller: lock="z" keeps it in a plane, gravity and jump as above) or "top_down" (no gravity, no jump). The page feeds move.x/move.z from WASD or the stick, a
jump press and a jump axis from Space/C or the pad's A, and camera.yaw from where the player looks; declare game.input@1(name="move", axis="x,z", target="tag:hero") and
game.input@1(name="jump", key="press", target="tag:hero"). The hero gets props grounded and speed for animation rules. VIEW: game.camera@1(name="behind", mode="third", distance=5,
height=1.6, shoulder=0.5, smoothing=0.08) follows tag:hero (mouse orbits it); modes first, third, top_down, side (dead zone, bounds="x0,x1,z0,z1"), iso, fixed (at="x,y,z", watches the
target). The first camera starts; game.rule@1(on="start", do="effect:camera:above:1.5") blends to the camera named above in 1.5 s (no seconds = a cut). A rule's every= is in seconds (on="tick" every=8 fires every eight seconds), so two camera rules with every= make the view switch back and forth for good; switch on an event instead. Example: web/tests/scenes/walker/walker.txt.
FALLING: game.controller@1(fall_limit=-8) with game.ground@1(y=-30) puts the hero back on the last safe ground when it falls below -8 m and raises the event fell: game.rule@1(on="fell", do="add:lives:-1"). Animation: a controlled hero tells its animation machine speed (number), grounded and jumping (flags) and the triggers jump and land, with no rules.
CONTROLS: game.input@1(name="jump", key="press", target="tag:hero", keys="Space,KeyC", pad="button0", label="Jump") names the keys (KeyboardEvent codes) and gamepad controls (button<N>, stick:left, stick:right, axis<N>+/-) of an input; an axis input needs a positive and a negative key per axis: axis="x,z" keys="KeyD,KeyA,KeyW,KeyS" pad="stick:left". The player can rebind keys; inputs named move and jump get WASD/stick and Space/C/A when you name none. Enter and the d-pad/A work menus on their own.
FLOW: game.state@1(name="title", frozen=true) declares states (the first is where the game starts; a frozen one stops everything except presses: title, paused, game_over, win; the states named win and game_over are entered by the goals). Limit a rule to one with game.rule@1(on="input:pause", state="playing", do="go:paused"); every rule on an event sees the state the event began in, so one key can pause in playing and resume in paused. Actions: go:STATE, restart or restart:STATE (rebuild the game and enter the state), level:NAME (game.level@1(name="cave") + game.spawn@1(level="cave"): swaps the level's entities and puts heroes at its start), checkpoint and respawn. Entering a state raises state:NAME, loading a level level:NAME. The page keeps save slots, undo and settings.
SCREEN UI: game.ui@1 draws the game's menus and HUD over the view with a procedural font (no assets). type is text, bar, panel, button, stack, grid or minimap. A stack places its children (parent="menu"): game.ui@1(name="menu", type="stack", anchor="c", align="center", gap=0.03, pad=0.05, fill="rgba(8,12,20,0.8)", show="title") then game.ui@1(name="play", type="button", parent="menu", text="Play", size="0.3,0.075", do="go:playing"). Text binds variables and keys: text="Score {score}   {key:jump} to jump". Bars: type="bar", value="hp" (a variable), max=100 or max_var="hp_max", size="0.3,0.03". Letter height is letter=0.04. show="paused,title" limits an element to flow states. Buttons raise ui:NAME; arrows and the d-pad move the focus, Enter and A press it, a click presses; tip="..." shows under the focused button. Minimap: type="minimap", size="0.2,0.2", radius=30, follow="tag:hero", tags="coin,enemy". Write colours as rgba(r,g,b,a) or quoted "#rrggbb". Example: web/tests/scenes/platformer/platformer.txt.
SHOOTING: game.health@1(kind="turret", hp=30, iframes=0.3, knock=3) gives a kind hit points (props health, max_health); game.projectile@1(kind="bolt", speed=26, life=1.5, damage=10, pierce=0, splash=0, homing=0, gravity=0) makes a kind a shot that flies, hurts the first victim, stops at solid walls and raises hit and impact; game.weapon@1(name="blaster", mode="projectile", shot="bolt", input="fire", reload_input="reload", owner="tag:hero", ammo=16, reload=1.2, cooldown=0.2, spread=1.5, aim="camera", auto=true) fires it (mode="hitscan" with range and damage is an instant ray). aim: heading, camera (through the crosshair of game.camera@1), or a selector such as tag:enemy (toward the nearest). An enemy weapon has input="none" and a rule fires it: game.rule@1(on="tick", every=2.5, do="fire:spit"). Rule actions hurt:SELECTOR:AMOUNT (optionally @SOURCE), heal:SELECTOR:AMOUNT, fire:WEAPON, reload:WEAPON; events hurt, killed (the entity is removed after the rules hear it), fired, empty, reloaded, hit, impact. The magazine is the owner's prop ammo_NAME, so a bar or text can show it: game.ui@1(type="bar", value="hero.health", max_var="hero.max_health") and text="Ammo {hero.ammo_blaster}". Example: web/tests/scenes/arena/arena.txt.
PARTY COMBAT: game.brain@1(kind="knight", foes="tag:enemy", leader="tag:hero", speed=4.6, follow=3, engage=20, weapon="sword") makes a kind follow its leader and fight on its own (companions and enemies); keep=9 stands a ranged fighter off. game.weapon@1(mode="melee", range=2.4, arc=110, damage=95, foes="tag:enemy", aim="heading"|"tag:enemy") swings at everything in the arc; foes keeps allies from hurting each other (also for shots and rays). game.targeting@1(leader="tag:hero", foes="tag:enemy", range=30) keeps the hero's target (prop target; the foe's prop targeted is 1) and the rule action target:next cycles it. game.ability@1(name="smash", owner="tag:hero", input="power1", cooldown=12, range=5, needs_target=true, do="hurt:b:320") runs actions with a = the owner, b = its target, and counts the owner's prop cd_smash down; refused:smash is raised when it cannot work. Actions: blast:CENTRE:RADIUS:AMOUNT[@FOES] (blast:a:4.5:170@tag:enemy), dash:a:11:0.25 and iframes:a:0.45 (a dodge), heal:tag:party:260. Screen elements: game.ui@1(type="slot", value="vriden.cd_smash", max_var="vriden.cdmax_smash", icon="sword", key="{key:power1}") an ability square with a cooldown, type="portrait" (text="V", fill=colour), type="floaters" (damage numbers, +healing and Dodge! over the heads of what was hurt: one per game), and when="targeted.health>0" shows a target frame only while something is targeted ({targeted.health}, value="targeted.health"). A game with many nodes is gathered in groups: game.collect@1(...) of kinds, spawns, weapons and the controller together (they are checked against each other), another of screens, and an outer collect of the groups. Example: web/tests/scenes/party/party.txt.
CREATURES: a kind with an agent patrols, notices the hero, chases and can be stunned: game.agent@1(kind="scuttler", patrol=[[-3, 12], [3, 12], [3, 18]], speed=1.4,
chase_speed=2.6, sight=6, lose=10). It walks on what game.nav@1(parts=["floor", "ramp"], cell=0.25, radius=0.35) names (the output names of the walkable parts; with no nav
line it walks straight through walls). Events a rule can use: sight, lost, stun, recover, catch (a = the creature, b = the hero): game.rule@1(on="catch",
do="add:lives:-1;stun:a:3;effect:anim:alert@a"), game.rule@1(on="stun", do="effect:anim:stagger@a"). stun:SELECTOR:SECONDS freezes creatures for that long. A
creature kind draws as a model when its part is an animated hierarchy (parts that anim.parent each other, plus an anim.machine): every creature is its own copy
with its own walk cycle, turned to face where it goes, and effect:anim aimed at a creature reaches only that one. A skinned character (body.human with body.skin, body.outfit, rig.skin
eyes) is a creature too: the kind's part is the skeleton root, which carries the anim.machine and one track per clip the machine names (a small bob is enough); the bones
chain to it with anim.parent, but never anim.parent a skinned part itself (rig.skin_not_rigid: its skin is dropped). The skinned parts join the copy through the bones they follow. effect:particles:NAME@b bursts at b
(explode, sparks, smoke, dust, fire, splash, magic, steam, embers).

ROLLING THINGS AND HAND-HELD TOOLS (golf, billiards, bowling, hockey, tennis ... any game where something rolls on the ground and a hand hits it): the ground a thing
rolls on is built from the parts you name: game.terrain@1(parts=["course", "green"], cell=0.2) (the OUTPUT names of the authored parts that are walkable ground: their top
surface is the ground, anywhere no part covers is void and a rolling thing over it is out). game.surface@1(name="sand", parts=["bunker"], decel=8, bounce=0.1) says what a
rolling thing does on the footprint of those parts: decel is how fast it slows in m/s2 (a fast green 0.55, short grass 1.0, rough 3, sand 8; a billiard cloth about 0.3), bounce
how much of a bounce it keeps; later surfaces win where parts overlap, and anywhere else is decel 1.0. A rolling thing: game.kind@1(name="ball", size=0.03, roll=true,
bounce=0.3, part="ball_mesh"): it falls, bounces, rolls, runs down slopes and rests. A hand-held tool (club, cue, bat, racquet, mallet): game.kind@1(name="putter", size=0.05,
tags=["hand_r"], swing=true, reach=0.9, loft=0, power=1.0, part="putter_mesh") with game.input@1(name="tool", follow="right_hand", target="tag:hand_r"): its head is reach
metres out of the hand along the hand's -Z axis, and a swing whose head passes through a rolling thing hits it with the head's speed (times power, at most 45 m/s) along
the swing, tilted up by loft degrees (flat 0, a wedge-like 50). Model the tool so its grip is at the part's origin and its shaft and head run out along -Z (the part is drawn
turned with the hand). On a desktop the right hand floats in front of the view and the tool points where you look: aim by looking at the ball, swing by turning the view
quickly. A pocket (a hole, a net, a cup, a pocket of a table): game.kind@1(name="cup", size=0.07, pocket=true) spawned where it is: a rolling thing over it slower than
1.6 m/s raises pocket (a = the pocket, b = the thing): game.rule@1(on="pocket", do="add:holes:1;destroy:b;effect:sfx:powerup@a"); a swing raises swing:
game.rule@1(on="swing", do="add:strokes:1"); a rolling thing that leaves the ground raises out (a = the thing). To send the player somewhere (the next tee, the
other end of the table): effect:message:goto_X_Y_Z_LX_LZ (feet at X, Y, Z looking at LX, LZ), and spawn the next ball with spawn:ball@x,y,z. A game of this kind
needs a score or count in the HUD and something to do after each pocket; keep a variable for the stage (add:hole:1) and give each stage its own pocket position.

Check it, do not trust it: game_describe prints what the document defines; playtest(policy="seek:hero:pickup") walks a bot to the nearest pickup and
reports won, lost or playing, the final variables and never_fired (rules no play reached: usually a wrong tag). playtest(policy="idle")
should lose by a clock goal, or run out the steps. A game that no policy wins, or a rule in never_fired, is a design bug to fix before building more.
For a hand-held tool striking a rolling thing, call playtest({policy: "aim:ball:cup1,cup2,cup3"}): it reads the live positions and ground profile,
swings the right hand frame by frame, waits for rest or stage progress, and adapts the speed for up to 14 shots per target. It reports status,
strokes per target, shots taken, the last shot plan and whether the game was won; this policy runs in the viewer and can take several minutes.
Errors name the node that wrote the bad item (game.rule, game.kind, game.duplicate, budget.kinds ...).
topics.survey:
survey plans where a person can stand and look to see the evaluated scene. It samples all drawn triangle surfaces, tests floor headroom, spaces standing points, and greedily picks cameras that cover reachable samples at good quality. Coverage is the fraction of samples reachable by any candidate, not a guarantee that every surface of the level is visible. Walls are two-sided. Plans are deterministic for the same geometry and options. When there is nowhere to stand, the plan is an aerial ring.

mode is "auto" (default), "walk" or "orbit", also in snapshot {tour:{mode:"orbit"}}. Auto walks only on connected floor regions of at least 12 m2 in the lower 60% of the scene height (or at the base of a scene under 6 m tall), dropping roof and small elevated regions; otherwise it orbits. Walk stands wherever clearance permits, falling back to orbit only when nowhere is standable. Orbit always uses low and high aerial rings looking at the scene centre. The answer's mode reports "walk" or "orbit", whichever was actually used.

survey {} defaults: eye_height 1.65 metres, spacing 4 metres, max_views 12, yaws 8, target_coverage 0.95. Ranges: eye_height 0.1 to 5; spacing 0.25 to 100; max_views integer 1 to 64; yaws integer 1 to 32; target_coverage 0 to 1. Additional runtime/tour options: fov_deg 10 to 170 (default 90), pitch_deg -89 to 89 (default 6, positive up), max_distance 0.1 to 1000 metres (default 30), samples_per_m2 0.01 to 20 (default 2), seed integer 0 to 9007199254740991 (default 7). All numbers must be finite.

The answer contains cameras [{position,target,label}], coverage, predicted (coverage after each camera), standable_points, surface_samples, triangles, ms and skipped_instances. Geometry is the committed evaluated mesh, before live animation/physics offsets, as with measure. Instances are realized at their authored world transforms within a 200,000 instance-triangle budget; skipped_instances counts omitted placements. Disconnected qualifying floor regions are retained in Auto; Walk retains all standable areas. snapshot_args is {cameras:[...]} for the first six cameras: pass that object directly to snapshot.

snapshot {tour:true} plans and captures the default survey. tour may instead be an options object, for example {tour:{max_views:8,spacing:3}}. Tour max_views is 1 to 12; output contains up to two sheets with at most six labelled cameras per image. The previous camera is restored after each sheet, including on capture failure. image:false omits pictures. tour cannot be combined with camera, cameras, views, times or states. To inspect more than twelve planned views, call survey and pass successive groups of six cameras to snapshot.
topics.operator_reference:
list_operators

The operators you may use. By default a compact index: one line per operator with its inputs, output, parameters (type, range, unit, default) and what it does, grouped by family, plus the ready-made kits. Narrow it with query (words in the id or help) or family (solid, poly, inst, xform, value ...). Pass ids=["solid.box@1", "kit.door"] to get the full documentation of just those (a kit returns its source), or detail="full" for everything (large).

Parameters:
query: Words that must appear in the operator id or help, for example "scatter surface".
family: Only this family: the part of the id before the dot, such as poly or inst.
ids: Full specs of exactly these operator ids (for example solid.box@1) or kits (kit.door).
detail: index (default) is one line per operator; full is every operator with all parameter documentation.
topics.find_reference:
find

Finds nodes in the document without reading all of it. query: words that must appear in a label, id, operator or parameter (name or value); family: only operators of that family (solid, inst, terrain, game ...); node: one node by label or id, answered in full with what feeds it, what uses it and the scene output it is. Matches come as one-line forms in the text language plus labels, so you can keep talking in names.

Parameters:
query: {"type":"string"}
family: {"type":"string"}
node: A label or id: one node, with its inputs and users.
limit: Most matches to return (default 30).
topics.script_api:
script

Runs BEHAVIOUR you write, in JavaScript, against the running world: anything the nodes cannot say (spin a part, follow another, react to a time, drive many parts every frame). action start (with name and source), stop, list or logs. Each script runs in its own worker (no network, no page access) and is stopped if one frame takes over 250 ms. The source is the body of an async function with these names: world.parts() (the authored parts: {entity, name, node}), world.get(entity, "Transform") and world.set(entity, "Transform", value) (an entity is a part name or an id; a Transform is {translation:[x,y,z], rotation:[x,y,z,w], scale:[x,y,z]}, an offset from where the part was built), world.batch([{method, params}, ...]) (up to 512 world calls in one request: do this for anything you change every frame), world.call(method, params) (any method of the world tool), on("frame", (dt, t) => ...) (every frame; dt and t in seconds), on("click", e => ...) and on("click:crate_left", e => ...) (events: hover, unhover, press, release, click, grab, drop, each with e.part the part name and e.pointer; and game.message, game.sfx, game.particles ... for a game rule effect, with e.part the name given to the effect: a rule effect:message:shot@a is heard by on("game.message:shot")), every(seconds, fn), log(...) (read with action logs), time(), random() (seeded: Math.random is the same). Reads and writes answer on the next frame, so write the NEW value from your own variables (keep state in a variable), do not read-modify-write in a loop. A part that has animation tracks or a parent has its Transform overwritten by the animation, so script static parts. Check what the script does with snapshot (times or states), and read its logs and errors. Scripts last until stopped or the page reloads.

Parameters:
action: {"type":"string","enum":["start","stop","list","logs"]}
name: Lowercase letters, digits and underscores.
source: The script body (for start).
topics.snapshot_modes:
snapshot

For a planned tour use tour:true or tour:{max_views:8}; see get_guide topic survey.

Looks at the view: returns a small picture (JPEG, up to 512 px wide) of what the editor shows, plus what changed since the last snapshot with the same name (share of the view that changed, where, and a box around it). Take one after an edit to check it did what you meant; pass image=false to get only the comparison, the cheapest way to ask whether an edit changed anything on screen. Use the same camera for comparable snapshots. Pass camera={position:[x,y,z], target:[x,y,z]} for one picture from an explicit camera; pass cameras=[{position:[0,5,5], target:[0,0,0], label:"air"}, ...] (1 to 6) for ONE labelled contact sheet in reading order, with the same two-column layout as views. Positions and targets are three finite numbers in metres; missing labels become camera 1, camera 2, etc. camera and cameras cannot be combined with each other or with views, times or states. Explicit cameras use their targets directly and do not need scene bounds; focus applies to named views and motion only. Each mode restores the previous view afterwards. Pass views (front, back, side, left, top, iso; up to 6) for one contact sheet of the scene from those angles at equal distance, each cell labelled; focus names a single part to look at instead of the whole scene. To SEE MOTION pass times (seconds, up to 8: the animation clock is paused at each and one picture shows every moment) or states (up to 8 objects of state-machine parameters, for example [{"speed":0},{"speed":1.5}]: each is set, the machine runs for a second and one picture shows them side by side), with view (default side) and focus; a walk you wrote is not verified until you have looked at it this way.

Parameters:
camera: One explicit position and target; optional label. Captures and compares with the named baseline.
cameras: 1 to 6 explicit cameras with optional labels, in reading order, in one sheet.
times: Motion sheet: seconds into the animation, one frame each (up to 8).
states: Motion sheet: state-machine parameters per frame, for example {"speed": 1.5} or {"grounded": false}; each frame lets the machine run for a second.
view: The camera of a motion sheet (default side).
views: Named cameras for a contact sheet, in reading order.
focus: A part name: the contact sheet looks at this part only.
name: Which earlier snapshot to compare with (default "last"); use different names to keep separate baselines.
image: false returns only the comparison, without the picture.
width: Picture width in pixels, 64 to 512 (default 512).
topics.edit_diff:
edit {ops, label?, dry_run?} compiles all operations to one atomic typed-command batch. set {node, params} updates parameters; rename {node, to} changes a unique label; delete {node} removes that node (remove its users first if needed); replace {node, text} replaces one node using one text-language node statement, preserving downstream links, outputs and flags. The replacement statement must use the original label. Labels resolve in operation order, so later operations can use a renamed label. Duplicate or unknown labels are errors listing candidates. No operation is sent until every operation has been checked. Evaluation and dry_run use the same path and delta as apply_text.

diff {since?} reads retained revision documents without undoing or changing the document. since is a non-negative safe integer, defaulting to the previous revision (or the current revision if no earlier revision exists). It returns compact lines prefixed + (added), ~ (changed) or - (removed), at most 80 lines plus the count of remaining lines. An unavailable revision reports the retained range; opening or resetting a document starts new history. Undo and redo are revisions too.
topics.creatures:
Creatures and bodies. Any body is built from the same few pieces; choose the technique by how the thing moves.

1. Hard parts that turn on joints (robot, mech, vehicle, crab shell): ordinary solids joined with anim.parent, each joint an anim.track or
   anim.wave with pivot at the joint (topics behaviour and animation). No skinning.
5. A released object (magazine, tool, shell casing): use anim.drop to bake gravity, floor bounce and rest into position keys; add spin for a turn about the part's centre.
2. Legs that plant feet (spider, insect, quadruped, walker): a bone chain per leg and rig.ik, with a small TARGET shape at each foot that
   you animate. The legs follow the targets. For a two-bone limb (arm, human or animal leg) add solver="two_bone" and a pole: pole=[0, 0, 1]
   makes a knee point forward (+z) and never flip; soften=0.3 eases the limb in before it locks straight (no popping knee); twist rolls
   the knee or elbow. Other chain lengths (tentacles, tails) keep the default solver.
   To make a head, eye or turret LOOK at something: rig.aim@1(target_shape, bone="head") on a small target; the bone turns so its
   head-to-tail direction points at the target and its up stays towards the pole (default [0, 1, 0]).
   To let a bone-built character go LIMP (death, a hard hit): put phys.ragdoll@1(marker, name="hero", bones="pelvis; spine; head; arm_l; forearm_l; ...",
   hinges="forearm_l; shin_l", swing=60, twist=25) on any small shape, bones listed parents first (each a rig.bone part, anim.parent-ed to its parent), and
   give the floor and walls phys.body kind="static". In play mode, world physics.ragdoll {name:"hero", impulse:[0,0,-40]} drops it from the pose it is in.
3. Soft limbs (tentacle, tail, spine, vine, snake): ONE tube skinned to a chain of bones that wave with a phase offset along the chain.
4. A smooth whole body in one call: make_character(plan="biped"|"quadruped"|"serpent") or a custom creature = { bones, blobs } (topic
   characters). Edit the graph it writes if you want to change a part.
Mix them: a horror is a lumpy body (solid.sphere + xform.scale) with technique 3 tentacles and glowing eyes; a robot is technique 1 with
technique 2 legs.

Things that go wrong (each of these was a refused edit or a black picture while testing):
- A list of points is nested: points=[[0, 0, 0], [1, 2, 0]]. A flat list is refused with "expected a point".
- Every bone and every skinned mesh must be an OUTPUT, and anim.parent / rig.ik / rig.skin name the OUTPUT names, not the node names.
  Write the output line right after the bone: output leg0_upper = leg0_up_bone.
- Bones are listed root first. A bone's head is where it turns; the next bone's head equals this bone's tail. Coordinates are world
  coordinates at rest.
- Without a light the scene is black. Add sky = scene.sky@1(sun_elevation=32, sun_azimuth=40, sun_intensity=4) and output sky = sky.
  The ground needs a surface too: a flat solid.box with solid.material.
- At most 32 bones in one rig.skin. Several skins are fine (one per tentacle).
- A document holds at most 64 NAMED OUTPUTS ("too many named outputs"), and every bone, skinned mesh, IK target and visible part is
  one. A spider (8 legs of upper, lower and target) uses 26; a horror with six 6-bone tentacles uses 46, so the two do not fit in one
  document: give a horror four tentacles, or keep one big creature per document. Plan the bone count against 64 before you write it.
- Repeated parts are written out: generate the lines for leg 0 to leg 7 yourself with the numbers changed (a spider with 8 legs is 112
  lines, a six-tentacle horror 260). apply_text takes up to 256 KiB.

Recipe, one IK leg (copy it per leg; hip on the body edge, knee up and out, foot on the ground y = 0). A spider has 8, around the
body at angles (i + 0.5) / 8 * 360 degrees:
  leg_up_path = curve.polyline@1(points=[[0.277, 0.75, 0.115], [0.785, 1.1, 0.325]])
  leg_up_tube = curve.tube@1(leg_up_path, radius=0.05, end_radius=0.035, sides=10)
  leg_up_paint = solid.material@1(leg_up_tube, color=[0.12, 0.1, 0.1], roughness=0.5)
  leg_up_bone = rig.bone@1(leg_up_paint, head=[0.277, 0.75, 0.115], tail=[0.785, 1.1, 0.325])
  output leg_upper = leg_up_bone
  leg_lo_path = curve.polyline@1(points=[[0.785, 1.1, 0.325], [1.34, 0.02, 0.555]])
  leg_lo_tube = curve.tube@1(leg_lo_path, radius=0.035, end_radius=0.012, sides=10)
  leg_lo_paint = solid.material@1(leg_lo_tube, color=[0.12, 0.1, 0.1], roughness=0.5)
  leg_lo_bone = rig.bone@1(leg_lo_paint, head=[0.785, 1.1, 0.325], tail=[1.34, 0.02, 0.555])
  leg_lo_child = anim.parent@1(leg_lo_bone, parent="leg_upper")
  output leg_lower = leg_lo_child
  foot = solid.sphere@1(radius=0.03, segments=8)
  foot_at = xform.move@1(foot, by=[1.34, 0.02, 0.555])
  foot_step = anim.wave@1(foot_at, property="position", amplitude=[0, 0.18, 0], base=[0, 0.18, 0], period=1.2, shape="triangle", phase=0)
  leg_reach = rig.ik@1(foot_step, bones="leg_upper; leg_lower")
  output leg_target = leg_reach
Gait: give neighbouring legs phase 0 and 0.5 (alternating), so half the feet are down at any moment. The legs stepped in place in the
test. A walk that travels (body and targets moving forward together) was not tried.

Recipe, one tentacle (six bones on a curved path; a horror has several):
  path = curve.polyline@1(points=[[0.7, 0.45, 0], [0.95, 0.94, 0], [1.2, 1.34, 0], [1.45, 1.59, 0], [1.7, 1.64, 0], [1.95, 1.49, 0], [2.2, 1.16, 0]])
  dense = curve.resample@1(path, count=40)
  tube = curve.tube@1(dense, radius=0.16, end_radius=0.015, sides=10)
  skin_paint = solid.material@1(tube, color=[0.45, 0.16, 0.2], roughness=0.35)
  b0_box = solid.box@1(size=[0.03, 0.03, 0.03])      b0_at = xform.move@1(b0_box, by=[0.7, 0.45, 0])
  b0_rig = rig.bone@1(b0_at, head=[0.7, 0.45, 0], tail=[0.95, 0.94, 0])
  b0_wave = anim.wave@1(b0_rig, property="rotation", amplitude=[8, 0, 16], period=2.2, phase=0, pivot=[0.7, 0.45, 0])
  output t_bone0 = b0_wave
  (bone i: head = point i, tail = point i + 1, b1_child = anim.parent@1(b1_rig, parent="t_bone0") before its wave, phase = i * 0.09,
   pivot = its head, a little more amplitude toward the tip)
  skinned = rig.skin@1(skin_paint, bones="t_bone0; t_bone1; t_bone2; t_bone3; t_bone4; t_bone5", falloff=3, influences=2)
  output tentacle = skinned
The tube needs many rings to bend, which is why it is resampled to 40 points first. A different period and phase per tentacle makes
them writhe out of step. Eyes: solid.sphere with solid.material emissive=[1.2, 1, 0.2].

Detailed organic bodies (an octopus): build the surface as a FIELD, then mesh it once.
- Body: field.ellipsoid parts moved with field.move and joined with field.smooth_union (radius 0.1 to 0.3 blends them), then
  field.to_solid(min, max, edge_length). If the field touches the bounds it is refused with field.clipped and the point: enlarge min and max.
- Arm: field.tube(points=[...polyline...], radius=0.2, end_radius=0.03) along the arm's curve, then a cupped sucker row: for each sucker a
  small field.sphere moved onto the underside and field.smooth_union-ed in (the rim), then a smaller sphere moved slightly outward and removed
  with field.subtract (the cup). Fields have no rotate, so use spheres: they look the same from every side.
- Mesh ONE arm in its own frame, then copy it: xform.scale, then xform.rotate(angles=[0, yaw, 0]) per arm. xform.rotate about +Y maps
  (x, z) to (x cos(yaw) + z sin(yaw), -x sin(yaw) + z cos(yaw)); write each copy's bones at the same scaled and rotated positions, five
  bones per arm, each waving about its own head, and skin each copy to its own bones. The axis of an arm's bend is its local z turned by yaw:
  use amplitude [sin(yaw) * a, small, cos(yaw) * a].
- Keep skinned meshes small: an arm meshed at edge_length 0.025 broke into floating fragments (a skinned part past roughly 65 thousand
  vertices), at 0.036 it was clean. Prefer edge_length of 0.035 or more for an arm-sized skinned part; the body may be finer because it is
  not skinned. Tips thinner than the edge length dissolve into specks, so keep end_radius at about the edge length or more.
- Joints between a static body and skinned limbs show as a gap: the limbs are separate meshes. Close it by letting each limb START INSIDE
  the body (its first point well within the body volume, at the height of the body's lower sides) and by making the body low, with a thin
  wide field disc (a web) fused in with field.smooth_union so the limbs leave it instead of tucking under a brim. A hat-brim skirt with
  limbs hanging below it reads as a hat on stilts. Thicker limbs hide the seam better but mean more vertices: at base radius 0.25 the
  skinned arms broke up again at edge_length 0.036, at 0.17 to 0.22 they held.
- Order for looks: solid.material first, then solid.texture (a texture put before the material is overridden by its colour).
- Skin: use 3D noise, which follows the surface (a 2D expr noise showed triangular patches on a field mesh). The tested program, spotted
  skin: n = tex3d_fbm(noise=perlin, scale_x=3, scale_y=3, scale_z=3, iterations=4); base = tex3d_colorize(n, g=[0:#5e120c, 0.5:#a93b1d,
  1:#e08a58]); cell = tex3d_fbm(noise=cellular, scale_x=17, scale_y=17, scale_z=17, iterations=1); mask = tex3d_colorize(cell, g=[0:#000000,
  0.62:#000000, 0.68:#ffffff, 1:#ffffff]); spot = tex3d_colorize(cell, g=[0:#240407, 1:#4a0d0f]); fine = tex3d_fbm(noise=perlin, scale_x=28,
  scale_y=28, scale_z=28, iterations=2); albedo = tex3d_blend(spot, base, mask, blend_type=normal, amount=0.85); height = fine
  tex3d_colorize takes its gradient as g=[...], not gradient=. A texture program that fails to compile is not an error in apply_text: the
  part just shows without maps and the reason is only a console warning ("texture bake for the viewport failed"). If a texture does nothing,
  suspect the program.
- Eyes that look alive are layers, not one sphere: take a small sphere out of the head with field.subtract so the eye sits in a socket with a
  rim of skin, then stack an amber ball, a clear glossy cornea (solid.material opacity=0.16, roughness=0.02), a golden iris and a darker ring
  (spheres scaled to [1, 1, 0.3]), a black horizontal slit pupil (a sphere scaled to [1.05, 0.17, 0.3]) and a tiny emissive white glint.
- Eight arms of five bones with eight skins, two eyes with iris and pupil, a siphon and the mantle come to 56 outputs: close to the 64 limit.

More detail than the mesh edge allows:
- Relief inside the surface: field.noise@1(field, amplitude=0.02, scale=0.16, octaves=2, mode="ridged", seed=5) before field.to_solid. The surface
  moves by at most amplitude, so give the to_solid bounds that much room (else field.clipped). Its features need an edge_length of about a
  third of scale or finer; a field.to_solid over a whole creature is limited by the field-work budget (about 64 million units: an 8 m dragon
  meshes no finer than about 0.07 m), so use relief at scale 0.1 to 0.2 on big bodies and finer relief on small parts (a head, an eye ridge).
- Surface layers: solid.finish@1(part, clearcoat=0.6, clearcoat_roughness=0.08) for wet or lacquered skin, scales and eyes; translucency=0.4 for
  wings, leaves, ears and wax (light shows through); anisotropy for brushed metal and silk. Put it after solid.material.
- Relief in the pixel shader, finer than any mesh and free of texture memory: solid.finish@1(part, relief=0.6, relief_scale=22, relief_style="ridged")
  (smooth lumps, ridged creases, scales = round cells; relief_scale is features per metre: 8 bark, 30 lizard scales, 120 pores). It is
  tested on spheres and on a skinned dragon (a skinned part reads the noise at its rest position, so it should stay on the body as it
  moves; that I checked only in still frames). It replaces the toon look on that part, so build a relief creature without solid.toon.
- A low-poly body carrying fine detail: hi = field.to_solid (fine edge) of the noisy field; lo = poly.to_solid(poly.unwrap_uv(poly.decimate(poly.from_solid(hi),
  ratio=0.05))); baked = bake.maps(lo, hi, size=1024, maps="normal", max_distance=0.1, rays=32). It runs, but decimating a noisy mesh keeps its
  jagged silhouette, so decimate a smooth version (the field without noise at a coarse edge) as the low mesh and bake the noisy one onto it;
  poly.unwrap_uv reported poly.uv.stretched on the noisy sphere, so add seams or use method=angle.

Secondary motion (a tail, ear, antenna or hair that lags the body and springs back): build the chain as bone parts exactly as for a
tentacle or rig.ik (each bone anim.parent-ed to the one before, the first one to the body part, each starting where the last ends, all
outputs), skin a tube to them, and attach rig.secondary to the TIP bone:
  tip = rig.secondary@1(tip_bone, bones="tb0; tb1; tb2", stiffness=0.15, damping=3, gravity=3)   output tb2 = tip
stiffness 0 hangs free (hair), 0.3 a tail; gravity 0 floats. A spring simulation runs every frame in the viewer (ve-chain), so the chain
follows whatever moves the body (an anim.track, physics, a walk) with lag and springs back when it stops. The bones' own motion is replaced.
Tested with a body gliding back and forth and a three-bone tail: the tail trails and curves. At most 8 bones per chain, 8 chains in a scene.

Walking: a legged body walks when its body part MOVES and each leg's foot target is driven by rig.gait instead of by hand. Parent every
leg's top bone to the body (anim.parent(bone, parent="body")), give the body an anim.track (or physics, or a behaviour), build each leg as a
rig.ik chain as in the leg recipe above, and put rig.gait after rig.ik on the foot target:
  walk = rig.gait@1(reach_node, body="body", phase=0, stride_length=0.9, step_height=0.2, duty=0.6)   output leg0_target = walk
Each foot plants on the ground (ground=0 by default) while the body passes over it, then swings forward in an arc, never farther from its hip
than the leg's length. Give alternate legs phase 0 and 0.5 (spider), or 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 (four legs); stride_length is metres of body travel
per step cycle, duty the share of time on the ground (0.6 walk, 0.4 run, 0.8 creep). Tested: an 8-legged spider glides along a path and its
feet plant and step; the body's own path does not turn (feet follow the body's yaw, so rotate the body part to turn it). Each rig.ik or rig.gait
chain counts toward the scene limit of 24 chains.

A real person: do NOT sculpt a head from primitives (tried: it drifts to ape proportions). body.human@1 is a real, anthropometric human with a
face, from open CC0 data:
  person = body.human@1(gender=0.2, age=0.667, height=0.55, weight=0.45, muscle=0.55, stature=1.82, waist=0.84)
  skin = solid.material@1(person, color=[0.78, 0.57, 0.46], roughness=0.55)
  fin = solid.finish@1(skin, subsurface=0.5, translucency=0.15, sheen=0.1)      output person = fin
  eyes = body.eye@1(person, iris_color=[0.28, 0.4, 0.5], gaze=[0, 0, 1])        output eyes = eyes
Sliders run 0 to 1 (0.5 average): gender 0 male to 1 female, age 0 baby, 0.333 child, 0.667 young adult, 1 old; height, weight, muscle,
proportions, and african / asian / caucasian shares. stature, waist, hip, chest (metres) and mass (kg) FIT the body to real measurements,
changing as little as possible; a request the body cannot meet gets the nearest body and a human.fit_partial warning that says what was
reached. face="jawOpen=0.8; mouthSmileLeft=0.6; eyeBlinkLeft=1" sets any of 52 face actions (0 to 1) and local="l-upperarm-fat-incr=0.5;
nose-width1-incr=-0.3" any of 256 local changes (-1 to 1; the nose, eyes, mouth, ears, chin, neck, torso and limbs each have some; a wrong name
lists the valid ones). The body is a polygon mesh (13,700 vertices, UVs
included), so every poly.* node takes it. It stands on y=0 facing +z, about 27,000 triangles; body.eye needs the body.human node itself as
input (before solid.material). cupsize and firmness (0 to 1) shape the bust; at=[x, y, z] and turn=degrees place and turn the person (the eyes and
hair follow). For fuller hips ask for a bigger hip (1.15 m) and add local="hip-scale-horiz-incr=0.8; buttocks-volume-incr=0.7".
Hair: body.hair@1(person, length=0.22, density=0.6, volume=0.3, wave=0.25, fringe=0.3, width=0.016, seed=1) grows ribbon wisps from that head's
own scalp with a natural hairline (0.02 buzz cut, 0.15 bob, 0.3 past the shoulders, no longer than 0.35); colour it with solid.material and
solid.finish(sheen=0.1). Set fine=1 for individual narrow strands and cover=true to hide the scalp beneath a hair shell; connect the body.human node itself, like body.eye. Not yet there: eyebrows,
teeth and a separate beard.
ANIMATING A PERSON (real skeleton, real skin weights, fingers): body.bone@1(person, bone="upperarm01_l") makes a tiny hidden part at that joint, a
bone, with its rest segment from the joint to the next one. Name each bone's OUTPUT exactly like the bone (output upperarm01_l = ...), join each to
its parent with anim.parent (the nearest bone you animate above it), and turn it with anim.track (property="rotation", pivot = the bone's head,
keys in degrees about X, Y, Z applied Y then X then Z, in the rest frame; the parent's motion is applied on top). body.skin@1(person,
bones="root; spine01; ...; wrist_l; finger2_1_l") skins the body to the bones you list with the pack's own weights (up to 64 bones; a bone you
leave out hands its weight to its nearest listed ancestor, so the legs can stay with root). Bone names: root, spine05 to spine01, neck01 to neck03,
head, clavicle_l, shoulder01_l, upperarm01_l, upperarm02_l (twist), lowerarm01_l (elbow), lowerarm02_l (twist), wrist_l, finger1_1_l (thumb) to
finger5_3_l (little finger), upperleg01_l, lowerleg01_l, foot_l, toe1_1_l; the same ending _r for the right side (the body's right is -x). A skinned body cannot
carry its own tracks; solid.material goes after body.skin. Clothes: body.garment@1(person, cover="long_sleeves", offset=0.008, bones="<the same
list>", hem=true) cuts a shirt, trousers (cover="pants"), shorts or shoes (shirt, long_sleeves, pants, shorts, shoes, gloves) out of the body's own surface,
lifts it off the skin, makes clean planar waist and cuff edges, and skins it with the same weights; omit hem=true to keep the original ragged edge. Use fit="tailored", ease=0.03, folds=0.006, rim=0.002 for loose cloth with deterministic folds and a closed, thick hem; tailored fit ignores hem. Give it a fabric. Hold things by parenting them to a hand bone (anim.parent
parent="wrist_r"). The arms are not solved for you: compute the joint angles for where the hands must be (a two-bone solve plus a wrist) and write
them as keys; a finger curls about the axis across its direction and the palm. Every track of a looping clip must end at the same time, or the
 clip is as long as the longest track. For real clothes and hair use `body.outfit` (ADR 0056): `body.outfit(person, asset="female_casualsuit01", standoff=0.012, bones="..." )` fits the artist's T-shirt and jeans to the body and skins them with its weights, and `solid.texture(program="image(albedo="female_casualsuit01_diffuse", normal="female_casualsuit01_normal")")` gives it the artist's pictures; hair (`ponytail01`, `long01`) is cut out with `solid.foliage` on the picture's alpha. A worked example, a person reloading an AK, is worlds/ak_reload.txt.

Making it read as a character: asymmetry (different lengths, a missing or extra limb, uneven phases) reads as horror; clean symmetry reads as
machine or animal. solid.style@1(part, style="anime") gives cel shading and outlines (topic styles). To move a creature through a world,
combine it with physics and behaviours (topic behaviour).
topics.effects:
Particle effects. A shape that carries fx.emitter gives birth to small soft sprites that fly, fade and die; the effect sits at the middle of the
shape and follows it when the shape moves (anim.track, anim.parent, held in a hand). Put fx.* AFTER geometry nodes such as xform.move (they rebuild the
shape and drop it); material, anim.* and rig.* nodes keep it.

fx.emitter@1(shape, name, rate, burst, burst_at, lifetime=[a,b], speed=[a,b], direction, cone, shape, extent, size=[start,end], colour, colour_end,
alpha=[start,end], glow, blend, render, max_particles, delay, duration, loop) makes the emitter. Call it again on the result for a second emitter
(fire plus smoke plus sparks); give each a name. Then refine one by name (the last one when no name is given):
- fx.force(kind="turbulence"|"wind"|"gravity"|"drag"|"vortex"|"attractor", strength, vector, centre, radius, scale, speed): turbulence is swirling noise
  with no sources or sinks, the thing that makes smoke and fire look alive (strength 1 to 3, scale 0.5 to 2). Forces add up.
- fx.collide(reaction="bounce"|"stick"|"kill", restitution, friction, ground=<y>): particles meet the ground plane at height ground, and in play mode
  every phys.body of the scene too (sparks bounce off a crate and a wall, chips pile on a table).
- fx.trail(points, min_step) with emitter render="ribbon": each particle leaves a streak (sparks, comet tails, tracers, sword swooshes).
- fx.sub(parent, child, on="death"|"birth"|"collide", count): particles of one emitter spawn particles of another (a splash where each drop lands).

render="cube" makes each particle a small LIT box that tumbles (spin=radians per second): wood chips, stone shards, shell casings; set size to its edge
and colour to its paint. The world call fx.status lists every emitting part with how many particles each emitter has alive and the box they fill: use it to
check that an effect runs and where it goes.

Looks: blend="additive" adds light (fire, sparks, magic, lightning: with glow 3 to 8 and bright colours, the bloom does the rest); blend="alpha" is ordinary
transparency (smoke, dust, mist, rain). size=[start,end] and colour/colour_end/alpha=[start,end] change over each particle's life: fire shrinks and goes
from yellow-white to deep red; smoke grows and fades. glow multiplies the colour above 1.

Recipes (a small shape s at the place the effect comes from):
- Campfire: fx.emitter(s, name="fire", rate=90, lifetime=[0.5,1], speed=[0.6,1.4], cone=14, shape="disc", extent=[0.14,0,0], size=[0.34,0.06], colour=[1,0.7,0.2],
  colour_end=[0.7,0.08,0], alpha=[1,0], glow=3, blend="additive") then fx.force(kind="turbulence", strength=2.4, scale=1.4); add a smoke emitter (rate=24,
  lifetime=[2,3.2], size=[0.25,0.95], colour=[0.24,0.24,0.26], alpha=[0.55,0], blend="alpha") with a turbulence and a wind force.
- Sparks that bounce: fx.emitter(name="sparks", rate=16, lifetime=[1,2], speed=[2,4], cone=40, size=[0.05,0.05], colour=[1,0.8,0.3], glow=6, blend="additive",
  render="ribbon") then fx.force(kind="gravity"), fx.collide(reaction="bounce", restitution=0.45, ground=0), fx.trail(points=9).
- Explosion: rate=0, burst=200, lifetime=[0.4,1.2], speed=[3,9], cone=85, shape="sphere", extent=[0.2,0,0], blend="additive", glow=5, size=[0.5,0.1]; a second alpha
  emitter for smoke with a burst; fx.force(kind="drag", strength=2).
- Rain with splashes: a wide shape="box" emitter high up, direction=[0,-1,0], speed=[8,10], rate=400, render="ribbon" with fx.trail(points=3), fx.collide(reaction="kill",
  ground=0) and fx.sub(parent="rain", child="splash", on="collide", count=3); the splash emitter has rate=0, lifetime=[0.2,0.5], speed=[1,2], cone=70, fx.force gravity.
- A trail behind something that moves: put the emitter on the moving part (anim.track), rate=60, speed=[0,0.2], lifetime=[0.4,0.8], size=[0.15,0], blend="additive".
- Magic: shape="sphere", extent=[0.3,0,0], speed=[0,0.3], fx.force(kind="vortex", centre at the shape, strength=3, radius=1) and fx.force(kind="attractor", strength=2).

Limits: 16 emitters per effect, 64 emitting parts per scene, max_particles up to 20000 per emitter. Effects are drawn by the Bevy renderer (the viewer and the
headset path). They are visual: they do not push the player or physics bodies.
topics.sim:
Simulations. sim.program@1(in?, source, library, values, seed, rate, size) runs a program you write, live. There is no cloth node, flock node or hair node:
those are programs. The same text gives the same result on every machine.

A program is lines (or `;` separated). In a node's source write newlines as \n.
  sim name
  param gravity = vec3(0.0, -9.8, 0.0)        a number or vector you can change later (values="gravity=0,-3,0", sim.set_param)
  input mesh cloth                            a mesh given on the node's `in` (a poly.grid for a cape, a strip for hair, a line for a rope)
  input bone anchor                           the pose of the part with this output name (in a game: this copy's own part)
  state pos: vec3[cloth]                      an array with one value per element; sizes: a number, a param, or a mesh input (one per vertex)
  state vel: vec3[256]                        types: f32 vec2 vec3 vec4 bool
  kernel init each i in pos { ... }           runs once at the start (a kernel named init), for each element i
  kernel step each i in pos { ... }           runs for every element, every step
  kernel once_a once { ... }                  runs once per step (set up or measure)
  schedule step; repeat 8 { solve }; finish   the kernels to run each step, in order; repeat N for solver passes (1 to 1000)
  output particles pos                        draw a vec3 array as small tetrahedra (size=, up to 4,000), or
  output mesh pos                             move the vertices of the `in` mesh (the array is sized by the mesh input)

Inside a kernel: `let x = ...`, `x = ...`, `+= -= *= /=`, `if c { } else { }`, `for k in 0..8 { }` (constant bounds, at most 4096 turns),
state is read as pos[j] and written ONLY as pos[i] (your own element) or pos[i].y = ...
Values and operators: numbers, true/false, vec2/vec3/vec4 (vec3(1.0) fills all three), swizzles (p.xz, v.y), + - * / %, < <= > >= == !=, && || !.
Functions: abs sign floor ceil fract sqrt exp log sin cos min max pow atan2 clamp mix step smoothstep length distance dot cross normalize
select(cond, a, b), hash(a, b) and rand(a, b) (0 to 1, deterministic from the seed). Builtins: i (element), n (count of the kernel's array), dt, t, step, seed.
Neighbours: for j in neighbors(pos, p, radius) cap 24 { ... } visits the elements within radius of p, in index order, at most cap (cap is required).
Meshes: rest(m, i) where vertex i started; for j, len in adjacent(m, i) { ... } each vertex joined to i by an edge and the edge's rest length.
Bones: bone_point(anchor, p) carries a point from the bone's rest pose by its current pose; bone_vector(anchor, d) a direction.
Colliders: sdf_capsule(p, a, b, r) signed distance to a capsule (negative inside); closest_segment(p, a, b) the nearest point of the segment.
Springs: pull(p, q, rest) is the move that gives the distance between p and q its rest length (add half of it to each end, all of it to a pinned neighbour).
Ready-made: library="bridge" is 41 planks hung between two posts (set cut to a link number with sim.set_param and the bridge snaps there and falls in two
halves: web/tests/scenes/sim/bridge.txt); the same chain text makes ropes, chains and hair strands.

THE ONE RULE: a kernel reads the state as it was when the kernel started (plus its own writes to its own element) and writes only its own element.
So elements never race and the order they run in does not matter. A spring between two particles is therefore written from each end: each particle loops
over its adjacent vertices and moves itself (see the library cloth). A write to another element is refused at run time with the line.

Library: sim.program(in, library="cloth", values="pin_height=1.45; collider_radius=0.2; collider_top=0,1.1,-0.08; collider_bottom=0,0.7,-0.08") is a cape:
points above pin_height ride the bone named anchor; a capsule along the bone named body pushes the cloth out; params gravity damping relax pin_height collider_radius.
Name your bone parts anchor and body (rig.bone) or copy the plain-text program and rename the inputs.

Physics, both ways. `input bone crate` reads any part, including one a phys.body moves (play mode): bone_point(crate, p) is where the body carries p now. `output push crate push`
(push is a vec3 array) changes the speed of the dynamic body of the part crate by the SUM of the array each step, in metres per second: buoyancy, wind, a magnet,
a spring to somewhere. A program with only a push output still needs an `output particles` or `output mesh` to be drawn; draw a small probe marker. In a game each copy of a
model has its own body (crate#id) and its own program instance reading and pushing that body; a copy that leaves the game takes its body with it. Recipe:
web/tests/scenes/sim/buoyancy.txt (crates settle half under the water line; lift = 20 * depth fraction * dt gives a bobbing equilibrium with phys.body linear_damping 1.2).

Characters: put the simulation in the model of a game kind (its bones in the kind's hierarchy). Every copy the game spawns runs its OWN instance on its own
bones (a cape per soldier). Check with the world tool: sim.status lists one entry per part and per copy; sim.step {steps} runs them now; the fingerprint field
changes when anything in the state changes, so "did my edit change the simulation" is one comparison.

Errors name the line, the column and the fix: an undefined name (did you mean ...), a type mismatch, a neighbors loop without cap, a mesh program with no `in`,
more than 4,000 particles, a kernel that ran over 100,000 statements for one element. Start small (a few particles and one rule), run sim.step, read sim.status.

Recipe, a flock (web/tests/scenes/sim/murmuration.txt): state pos and vel, a flock kernel that loops over neighbours adding cohesion, alignment and separation to
an acceleration, a move kernel, schedule flock; move, output particles pos. Recipe, rain: pos[i].y -= speed * dt, and when it is below 0 put it back at the top using
rand(i, step) for its new x and z.
topics.limits:
Hard limits, what an error looks like and what to change. Numbers are checked against the engine's code by a test.
Budget errors say how far over you are and, for triangles, name the heaviest parts: fix those first. A failed edit changes nothing.

## The document
- nodes in one document: 5,000. To fix: build repeated things with groups, macros (def) or inst.* sets instead of one node per copy.
- nodes one evaluation expands to once groups and macros are unfolded: 20,000. To fix: fewer or smaller groups; a loop that makes 30 nodes per copy has a copy limit.
- named outputs (each is a part the renderer draws): 256. To fix: merge small props with solid.union or inst.realize, or place copies with inst.* instead of one output each.
- material definitions: 256. To fix: share one solid.material between parts.
- group definitions (groups may nest at most 8 deep): 256. To fix: flatten nesting; use macros for small repeated patterns.
- typed commands in one batch (a text program costs one per node, per input link and per output): 10,000. To fix: send a big world as several apply_text calls.
- undo steps kept: 200. To fix: none needed; older steps drop off.

## Geometry, memory, textures and lights
- memory one document's geometry and storage may need: 1 GiB (budget.memory). To fix: decimate (poly.decimate), lower detail, or split the scene.
- triangles stored or drawn: NO limit (memory is the bound); above 4,000,000 drawn it warns: 4,000,000 (warning only) (budget.drawn_heavy). To fix: lighter placed shapes or fewer placements.
- triangles in the whole scene for the ambient-occlusion bake (the real triangle ceiling): 1,000,000 (budget.ao_triangles). To fix: the error names the heaviest parts: lower their detail first (columns/rows/segments, a larger field.to_solid edge_length, less subdivision).
- cells in one field.to_solid grid (the bounds divided by edge_length, cubed): 6,000,000 (budget.field_cells). To fix: raise edge_length or shrink min and max; preview already uses twice the edge_length.
- work units to build one field (cells times the field's cost): 1,500,000,000 (budget.field_ops). To fix: raise edge_length or use fewer field primitives; noise and repeats cost the most.
- instructions in one field's compiled tape: 4,096 (budget.field_tape). To fix: split the field into parts, or simplify it.
- points in a field.tube path; a field repeat count: 128; 16. To fix: a tube with fewer points; build long repeats from two steps.
- placements in one instance set: 16,384 (budget.instances). To fix: lower count, count_x, count_y, count_z; split into several sets.
- lights in one scene (emissive parts that emit light count): 128 (budget.lights). To fix: remove emitters, or use emissive colour without emits_light.
- maps of baked textures on the GPU (1024, 512 and 256 px sizes share it): 192 MiB: 33 maps of 1024, or 136 of 512, or 546 of 256. To fix: give small things size="256" or "512" in solid.texture; share one texture between parts.
- a texture program's text: 8,192 bytes. To fix: simplify the program, or split it across two solid.texture nodes on two parts.

## Games and scripts
- entities alive at once: 2,048. To fix: despawn spent things (projectiles, effects); the game stops with an error at the limit.
